text: With the requirement written down, the next step is translating it into a plain-English plan -- what data this report needs, and where it actually lives -- before opening SSMS.

Thornbury runs on AdventureWorks2012, and this report needs five real tables, not four. Sales order detail holds the line totals and which product was sold. Sales order header holds the order date. Production dot Product holds the product, but only a subcategory ID -- not a category name directly. Production dot ProductSubcategory holds the subcategory, with a category ID. And Production dot ProductCategory finally holds the readable category name this report groups by. Category is two hops up from the product row, not one.

Written as a sentence first: start at the order detail, since that's where the dollar amounts live. Walk up to the order header for the date. Walk sideways to product. From there walk up to subcategory, then up again to category. Four join keys, each named before any real SQL exists: sales order ID, product ID, product subcategory ID, and product category ID.

Why start at the detail table and not the header? Because an order with three products on it produces three detail rows and only one header row. Starting from the table that holds LineTotal, the number actually being summed, and joining outward from there, avoids a classic mistake: double-counting an order's total once per line item.

One real nuance worth knowing up front: every join here is an inner join, which means a product with no subcategory assigned can never reach a category name, and drops out of the result. For a category performance report, that's correct behavior, not a bug -- this report only needs products that actually have a category.
With the tables, the joins, the filter, and the grouping all planned in plain English, next lesson turns this exact plan into real, runnable T-SQL against AdventureWorks2012.
